quote: Tversky and Kahneman recorded the estimates of subjects who saw the Wheel of Fortune showing various numbers.
content: Anchoring is, refreshingly, one of the most replicable findings in the heuristics-and-biases literature. The Wheel-of-Fortune paradigm and its descendants survived large-scale direct replication: Many Labs 1 (Klein et al. 2014) and Many Labs 2 (Klein et al. 2018) reproduced robust anchoring across dozens of labs and many thousands of participants. So unlike much of the social-cognition canon, the basic effect Yudkowsky describes here is on firm empirical ground.

quote: The current theory for this and similar experiments is that subjects take the initial, uninformative number as their starting point or anchor; and then they adjust upward or downward from their starting estimate
content: This "anchor-and-adjust" account is exactly the mechanism the next essay walks back. Epley & Gilovich (2006) showed deliberate adjustment occurs mainly for self-generated anchors; for the experimenter-provided numbers used in the Wheel-of-Fortune task, the effect is driven by selective accessibility (priming), not by sliding from a starting point and stopping early. Yudkowsky presents the adjustment story as "the current theory," then corrects it a chapter later, a sign the textbook narrative he is relaying was already outdated.

quote: Completely implausible anchors, such as 1215 or 1992, produced anchoring effects just as large as more plausible anchors such as 1905 or 1939.
content: Strack & Mussweiler's selective-accessibility result is real, but the "implausible anchors work just as well" claim needs qualification. Later work finds anchor extremity does matter: wildly implausible anchors produce smaller, not equal, effects in many designs (Wegener et al. 2001), and an anchor's pull depends on whether it is treated as relevant. The strong reading here, that even absurd numbers contaminate judgment to the same degree, overgeneralizes from a single demonstration.

quote: Tversky and Kahneman report that offering payoffs for accuracy did not reduce the anchoring effect.
content: The claim that incentives don't dent anchoring is often repeated but only partly true. Reviews of incentive effects (Camerer & Hogarth 1999) find financial incentives sometimes reduce biases, sometimes don't, and rarely eliminate them; anchoring is relatively incentive-resistant, but "did not reduce" is stronger than the evidence. Simmons, LeBoeuf & Nelson (2010) found incentives can reduce anchoring when they motivate people to think in the correct direction. The blanket statement papers over a more conditional result.
